lesson.title: Mapping the Path: Energy Diagrams
lesson.summary: A reaction energy diagram plots potential energy against reaction progress, showing the activation energy hill reactants must climb and revealing whether the overall reaction releases or absorbs energy.
lesson.body:
An energy diagram (also called a reaction coordinate diagram) is a graph, and like any graph, it has two axes: the horizontal axis, called the reaction coordinate or reaction progress, represents how far the reaction has advanced from reactants to products, while the vertical axis represents potential energy. Reading one is a direct application of graphing data to a chemistry problem: instead of plotting one variable against time, you are plotting energy against progress along a chemical transformation.

The diagram starts on the left at the potential energy of the reactants and ends on the right at the potential energy of the products. Between them sits a hill: energy rises to a maximum at a point called the transition state, or activated complex, a fleeting, unstable arrangement of atoms where old bonds are partially broken and new bonds are partially formed, before the system rolls downhill into the products. This hill is the graphical picture of activation energy: Ea for the forward reaction is the height of the hill measured from the reactants up to the peak, while Ea for the reverse reaction is the height of the same hill measured from the products up to that same peak. Because the peak is shared by both directions but the starting elevations differ, the forward and reverse activation energies are generally not equal to each other.

The difference between those two activation energies is exactly the overall energy change of the reaction, ΔH:

ΔH = Ea(forward) - Ea(reverse)

Let's use the numbers already established in the Arrhenius Equation chapter, where a forward activation energy of Ea = 75 kJ/mol was used in a worked calculation. Suppose the reverse reaction for that same process has an activation energy of 25 kJ/mol, meaning the products only need to climb 25 kJ/mol to get back over the same hill. Then:

ΔH = 75 kJ/mol - 25 kJ/mol = +50 kJ/mol

A positive ΔH means the products sit 50 kJ/mol higher on the diagram than the reactants: the reaction is endothermic overall, absorbing 50 kJ/mol as it proceeds, even though it still has to pay a much larger 75 kJ/mol admission fee just to get over the hill in the first place. If instead the reverse barrier had been larger than the forward barrier, ΔH would come out negative, and the diagram would show products sitting below reactants, an exothermic reaction.

One more feature worth marking on the diagram: a catalyst works by opening up an alternative pathway with a lower hill, lowering both Ea(forward) and Ea(reverse) by the same amount, which speeds up the reaction in both directions without changing the elevations of the reactants or products at all, and therefore without changing ΔH. On the graph, a catalyzed pathway looks like a second curve drawn beneath the original, same starting and ending points, lower peak in between.
